reading_pushes: Each feature 'pushes' XGBoost's prediction toward or away from what actually happened. Pushes are in log-probability units and add up to the gap between XGBoost's final prediction and its starting guess for an average ball. As a rough guide, a push of -0.3 cuts the chance of what happened by about a quarter, -0.7 roughly halves it, and -1.4 cuts it to about a quarter. These are the model's reasons for its prediction, not causes of what happened on the field.

A.title: Big hitters at boundary-friendly grounds aren't expected to run twos or threes
A.text: Ten balls ended in a three or a two, and XGBoost gave them almost no chance: 0.08-0.29% for the threes and 3.6-3.8% for the twos, against B1's 0.24-0.33% and 9.7-9.8%. On almost all of them, the biggest pushes against what happened came from the batter's history (above all how often he hits sixes) and from how often the ground gives up boundaries. Our hypothesis: the model has learned, correctly on average, that big hitters at small grounds score in boundaries and singles rather than twos and threes, so it moves probability away from twos and threes exactly when someone like Abhishek Sharma or V Suryavanshi is on strike. Threes are also rare for every model (about 0.3% of balls), and the label counts every run on the ball, so a three can be byes, leg-byes or an overthrow that no feature can see; part of each three is plain chance, and what XGBoost adds on top is its confidence in the batter's and the ground's profile.
A.check: S4b check A (H1): do batters in the top quarter for six rate run more twos and threes than XGBoost predicts across the 2026 death?

B.title: A new batter is expected to play himself in
B.text: Six sixes were hit by batters who had only just come in: five within their first three balls (at least two off the very first ball), and Kartik Tyagi before he or his partnership had scored a run. XGBoost gave them 1.9-3.8%, against B1's 5.1-10.7%. The new-batter state pushed hardest against the six: no runs yet in the partnership, and no balls or runs yet for the batter. Our hypothesis: in the training seasons a new batter usually took a ball or two before attacking, so the model cuts the six chance on a batter's first balls, while in 2026, when sixes rose to 8.5% of balls, more batters attacked straight away. For Shashank Singh and Washington Sundar, their own batting history pushed toward the six (+0.53 and +0.40), but the new-batter state outweighed it. For the lower-order batters (Kartik Tyagi, TA Boult, XC Bartlett, K Rabada), a weak strike rate at the death over the last three seasons pushed against the six as well, so the model was doubly sure.
B.check: S4b check B (H1): across the 2026 death, do batters in their first three balls, and batters at 8-11, hit more sixes than XGBoost predicts?

C.title: The last balls of an innings are read as an all-out slog
C.text: On the final one to four balls of an innings, and with nine wickets down, the scorecard features dominate: very few balls left per wicket in hand, the ball count itself (116-119 balls bowled), and the batting position of the striker and the non-striker. XGBoost read these balls as all-out slogs. It gave a dot on the last balls about 8-9.5%, where B1 gave 17-32% and the logistic regression 10-17%. For singles in the last four balls, a No. 9-11 at the non-striker's end also pushed the single down, as if the batter would refuse it to keep the strike. With nine down, a No. 10 or 11 hitting a four was rated 5.5-6.2% against B1's 8.4%. Our hypothesis: the finer scorecard, which brings most of XGBoost's gain at the death (82%), also makes it overconfident on the final balls, where batters still miss, defend, or take the single on offer.
C.check: S4b check C (H1): does XGBoost under-predict dots and singles across the 20th over of 2026 (not just on these balls)? If so, this also explains part of the season-wide under-prediction of death dots.

D.title: Wickets with no clear cause
D.text: Three wickets early in the death (15.1-15.6, with four or five down) cost XGBoost about 3.5-4% each, against B1's 7.4-7.7%. No feature pushed hard (the largest group push is -0.18), and the batters' own history pushed toward the wicket, not away from it. XGBoost simply gives a ball early in the death with wickets in hand a lower wicket chance than B1's coarser cell does, and across the season that lower chance is about right: balls it rates at 4-6% for a wicket are out about 4-5% of the time (figure 5). So we read these three as chance, the cost of being right on average, not as a feature that misled the model.
